items.title: 13.3 Pressure in a Gas and Derivation of PV = (1/3) Nm <v^2>

source_refs.note: Topic 13.3 with Examples 13.1-13.2 and two Brain Teasers, answered (PDF 6-9); Fig 13.2 is redrawn. Equation 13.14 printed as PV = (1/3)rho<v^2> is corrected in a warning. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Kinetic theory lets us derive an equation that links the macroscopic properties of a gas (pressure and volume) to the microscopic properties of its molecules (mass and speed). When gas molecules strike the walls of the container they exert a force on them, because their momentum changes in each collision. The pressure of a gas is the force per unit area on the walls caused by these collisions. The average kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, so raising the temperature increases the speed of the molecules, giving more collisions and a higher pressure.

An ideal gas obeys the gas law PV = nRT (13.1), where P is the pressure, n the number of moles, T the absolute temperature and R the general gas constant, R = NA kB. Here kB = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1 is the Boltzmann constant and NA = 6.02 x 10^23 per mole is the Avogadro number. Since the number of moles is n = N/NA, where N is the number of particles, PV = N kB T (13.2).

items: Consider one molecule of mass m in a cubical box of side L (Fig 13.2), moving with velocity component vx towards one face. It rebounds elastically with velocity -vx, so its change in momentum is dp = -mvx - (mvx) = -2mvx.
It travels a distance 2L between two hits on the same wall, so the time between collisions is t = 2L/vx (13.3).

By Newton's second law the average force on the molecule is the rate of change of momentum, and by Newton's third law the molecule pushes the wall with an equal and opposite force: F = 2mvx/(2L/vx) = mvx^2/L (13.4).
The wall has area L^2, so the pressure from this one molecule is P = F/L^2 = mvx^2/L^3 = mvx^2/V (13.5), where V = L^3.

For all the molecules, which have different speeds, P = (m/V)(v1x^2 + v2x^2 + v3x^2 + ...) (13.6). The average of vx itself is zero (half the molecules move each way), so we use the mean square <vx^2> = (v1x^2 + v2x^2 + ... + vNx^2)/N. Then P = N m <vx^2> / V. The square root of a mean square speed is the root-mean-square (rms) speed (13.8).
Since the molecules move randomly, they have the same average motion in all three directions: <v^2> = <vx^2> + <vy^2> + <vz^2> = 3<vx^2> (13.9, 13.10), so <vx^2> = <v^2>/3 (13.11).

blocks.alt: Left: an oblique sketch of a cube of side L with its right wall shaded orange; a molecule m in the middle has a red arrow vx towards the shaded wall and a blue arrow -vx back. Right: six steps, each a label and an equation: dp = -2mvx; t = 2L/vx; F = mvx^2/L; P = F/L^2 = mvx^2/V; for N molecules P = Nm<vx^2>/V; and with <v^2> = 3<vx^2>, PV = (1/3)Nm<v^2> in red.
blocks.caption: Pressure of a gas from molecular collisions (original diagram after Fig 13.2).
blocks.long_description: Each collision reverses the molecule's x-velocity. The faster the molecules move, the bigger the momentum change per hit and the more often they hit, which is why pressure depends on the square of the speed.

blocks.text: In terms of density: the density of the gas is rho = M/V = mN/V, where M = mN is the total mass, so the pressure equation can be written P = (1/3) rho <v^2> (13.14). It can also be written P = (2/3)(N/V)<(1/2)mv^2> = (2/3) No <K.E.>, where No = N/V is the number of molecules per unit volume.

blocks.title: Equation 13.14
blocks.text: The book prints equation 13.14 as 'PV = (1/3) rho <v^2>'. Since rho already includes the volume (rho = Nm/V), the correct form is P = (1/3) rho <v^2>, which is the form used in Example 13.1.

An ideal gas has a density of 4.5 kg m^-3 at a pressure of 9.3 x 10^5 Pa and a temperature of 504 K. Find the root-mean-square speed of the gas atoms. Solution: from P = (1/3) rho <v^2>, <v^2> = 3P/rho = 3 x (9.3 x 10^5 Pa)/(4.5 kg m^-3) = 6.2 x 10^5 m^2 s^-2. So v_rms = square root of 6.2 x 10^5 = 787 m s^-1, about 7.9 x 10^2 m s^-1.

What is the rms speed of air molecules (O2 and N2) at room temperature, 25 C? Solution: the masses are 32 u for O2 and 28 u for N2, with 1 u = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg, so m(O2) = 5.3 x 10^-26 kg and m(N2) = 4.6 x 10^-26 kg; T = 298 K and kB = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1. For oxygen, v_rms = square root of (3 kB T/m) = square root of (3 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 298 / 5.3 x 10^-26) = 481 m s^-1, about 4.81 x 10^2 m s^-1. Similarly, for nitrogen v_rms = 515 m s^-1. The speeds of air molecules are much greater than the speed of sound in air, about 340 m s^-1.

blocks.prompt: What is the difference between a mole and Avogadro's number? Does Avogadro's number depend on the state of the substance?
blocks.explanation: A mole is an amount of substance; Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23) is the number of particles in one mole. It is a constant and does not depend on whether the substance is a solid, liquid or gas.

blocks.prompt: How does kinetic theory explain Boyle's law and Charles's law?
blocks.explanation: From PV = (1/3)Nm<v^2> with <v^2> fixed by temperature: at constant T, PV is constant (Boyle's law), because a smaller volume means more frequent wall collisions; at constant P, raising T raises <v^2>, so V must increase in proportion to T (Charles's law).

items: PV = nRT = N kB T; R = NA kB.
One molecule: dp = 2mvx, t = 2L/vx, F = mvx^2/L.
Air molecules: about 480-515 m s^-1 at 25 C.
